## 3 The Maximum Theorem

The stage is now set for one of the most important theorems of optimization theory, the so-called Maximum Theorem.<sup>9</sup> 

The Maximum Theorem. Let Θ and X be two metric spaces, $\Gamma : \Theta \supseteq X$ a compact-valued correspondence, and $\varphi \in \mathbf { C } ( X \times \Theta )$ . Define 

$$
\sigma (\theta) := \arg \max \left\{\varphi (x, \theta): x \in \Gamma (\theta) \right\} \quad \text { for   all } \theta \in \Theta\tag{5}
$$

and 

$$
\varphi^ {*} (\theta) := \max \left\{\varphi (x, \theta): x \in \Gamma (\theta) \right\} \quad \text { for   all } \theta \in \Theta ,\tag{6}
$$

and assume that Γ is continuous at $\theta \in \Theta$ . Then: 

(a) $\sigma : \Theta \overset { } { \Longrightarrow } X$ is compact-valued, upper hemicontinuous and closed at $\theta _ { ; }$ 

(b) $\varphi ^ { * } : \Theta \to$ R is continuous at θ. 

Proof. Thanks to Weierstrass’ Theorem, $\sigma ( \theta ) \neq \emptyset$ for all $\theta \in \Theta$ , so $\sigma : \Theta \overset { } { \Longrightarrow } X$ is well-defined. Since $\sigma ( \theta ) \subseteq \Gamma ( \theta )$ for each θ, and $\Gamma ( \theta )$ is compact, the compactvaluedness of σ would follow from its closed-valuedness (Proposition C.4). The latter property ${ \mathrm { i s } } ,$ on the other hand, easily verified by using the closedness of $\Gamma ( \theta )$ and continuity of $\varphi ( \cdot , \theta )$ for each θ. (This is an easy exercise.) 

We wish to show that σ is closed at θ. To this end, take any $( \theta ^ { m } ) \in \Theta ^ { \infty }$ and $( x ^ { m } ) \in X ^ { \infty }$ such that $\theta ^ { m } \to \theta , x ^ { m } \in \sigma ( \theta ^ { m } )$ for each m, and $x ^ { m }  x$ . Claim: $x \in \sigma ( \theta )$ . Since Γ has a closed graph (Proposition 3), we have $x \in \Gamma ( \theta )$ Thus if $x \notin \sigma ( \theta )$ , then there must exist a $y \in \Gamma ( \theta )$ such that $\varphi ( y , \theta ) > \varphi ( x , \theta )$ . By lower hemicontinuity of Γ, then, we can find a sequence $( y ^ { m } ) \in X ^ { \infty }$ such that $y ^ { m } \in \Gamma ( \theta ^ { m } )$ for each $m _ { ; }$ , and $y ^ { m } \to y .$ . But since $( y ^ { m } , \theta ^ { m } )  ( y , \theta )$ and $( x ^ { m } , \theta ^ { m } )  ( x , \theta )$ , the inequality $\varphi ( y , \theta ) > \varphi ( x , \theta )$ and continuity of $\varphi$ force that $\varphi ( y ^ { m } , \theta ^ { m } ) > \varphi ( x ^ { m } , \theta ^ { m } )$ for m large enough.<sup>10</sup> Since $y ^ { m } \in \Gamma ( \theta ^ { m } )$ for each $m$ , this contradicts the hypothesis that $x ^ { m } \in \sigma ( \theta ^ { m } )$ for each $m .$ . Conclusion: $x \in \sigma ( \theta )$ 

Given its closedness at $\theta ,$ proving that σ is upper hemicontinuous at $\theta$ is now easy. Simply observe that $\sigma ( \theta ) = \Gamma ( \theta ) \cap \sigma ( \theta )$ for all $\theta \in \Theta$ , and apply Exercise 19. 

We now turn to assertion (b). Since $\varphi ( y , \theta ) = \varphi ( z , \theta )$ must hold for any $y , z \in \sigma ( \theta )$ $\varphi ^ { * }$ is well-defined on Θ. To prove that it is continuous at $\theta ,$ pick any $( \theta ^ { m } ) \in \Theta ^ { \infty }$ with $\theta ^ { m }  \theta$ . We wish to show that $\varphi ^ { * } ( \theta ^ { m } ) \to \varphi ^ { * } ( \theta )$ . Of course, $\left( \varphi ^ { * } ( \theta ^ { m } ) \right)$ has a subsequence, say $\left( \varphi ^ { \ast } ( \theta ^ { m _ { k } } ) \right)$ with $\varphi ^ { * } ( \theta ^ { m _ { k } } ) $ lim sup $\varphi ^ { * } ( \theta ^ { m } )$ . Now pick any $x ^ { m _ { k } } \in$ $\sigma ( \theta ^ { m _ { k } } )$ so that $\varphi ^ { * } ( \theta ^ { m _ { k } } ) = \varphi ( x ^ { m _ { k } } , \theta ^ { m _ { k } } )$ for each $m _ { k }$ . Since σ is compact-valued and upper hemicontinuous at $x ,$ we can use Proposition 2 to find a subsequence of $( x ^ { m _ { k } } )$ which we again denote by $( x ^ { m _ { k } } )$ for convenience, that converges to a point x in $\sigma ( \theta )$ By continuity of $\varphi _ { ; }$ , then 

$$
\varphi^ {*} (\theta^ {m _ {k}}) = \varphi (x ^ {m _ {k}}, \theta^ {m _ {k}}) \rightarrow \varphi (x, \theta) = \varphi^ {*} (\theta)
$$

which proves that $\varphi ^ { * } ( \theta ) = \operatorname* { l i m } \operatorname* { s u p } \varphi ^ { * } ( \theta ^ { m } )$ . But the same argument also shows that ϕ∗(θ) = lim inf $\varphi ^ { * } ( \theta ^ { m } )$  

Remark 1. [1] The lower hemicontinuity of $\sigma$ does not follow from the hypotheses of the Maximum Theorem. (For instance, let $X : = \Theta : = [ 0 , 1 ] = : \Gamma ( \theta )$ for all $\theta \in \Theta$ 2 define $\varphi \in \mathbf { C } ( [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 } )$ by $\varphi ( x , \theta ) : = x \theta$ . Then the solution correspondence $\sigma$ is not lower hemicontinuous at 0.) But ${ \mathrm { i f } } ,$ in addition to the assumptions of the Maximum Theorem, it is the case that there is a unique maximum of $\varphi ( \cdot , \theta )$ on $\Gamma ( \theta )$ for each $\theta ,$ then $\sigma$ must be a continuous function. For instance, if $X \subseteq \mathbb { R } ^ { n } , \Gamma ( \theta )$ is a convex set for each $\theta ,$ and $\varphi ( \cdot , \theta )$ is strictly quasiconcave on $\cup \Gamma ( \theta )$ , this situation ensues. (Recall Section A.4.6.) 

[2] Let $X : = \Theta : = \mathbb { R }$ , and define $\varphi \in \mathbf { C } ( X \times \Theta )$ by $\varphi ( x , \theta ) : = x$ . Consider the following correspondences from X into Θ: 

$$
\Gamma_ {1} (\theta) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} [ 0, 1), & \theta = 0 \\ \{0 \}, & \theta \neq 0 \end{array} \right. \quad \Gamma_ {2} (\theta) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} [ 0, 1 ], & \theta = 0 \\ \{0 \}, & \theta \neq 0 \end{array} \right. \quad \Gamma_ {3} (\theta) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \{0 \}, & \theta = 0 \\ [ 0, 1 ], & \theta \neq 0 \end{array} \right..
$$

Now define $\sigma _ { i } ( \theta )$ by (5) with $\Gamma _ { i }$ playing the role of $\Gamma , i = 1 , 2 , 3$ . Then, while $\sigma _ { 1 }$ is not a well-defined correspondence on Θ (because $\sigma _ { 1 } ( 0 ) = \emptyset )$ , neither $\sigma _ { 2 }$ nor $\sigma _ { 3 }$ are upper hemicontinuous at 0. Thus we need the compact-valuedness of Γ in the Maximum Theorem, and cannot replace the continuity of Γ with either upper or lower hemicontinuity. 

[3] By Proposition D.5, σ would be well-defined in the Maximum Theorem, if $\varphi$ was assumed only to be upper semicontinuous on $X \times \Theta$ . So it is natural to ask if continuity of $\varphi$ can be replaced in this theorem with upper semicontinuity. The answer is no! For example, let $X : = [ 0 , 1 ] , \Theta : = ( 0 , 1 ] , \Gamma ( \theta ) : = [ 0 , \theta ]$ for all $\theta \in \Theta$ and define $\varphi \in \mathbb { R } ^ { X \times \Theta }$ as 

$$
\varphi (x, \theta) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 - 2 x, & \text { if } 0 \leq x <   \frac {1}{2} \\ 3 - 2 x, & \text { if } \frac {1}{2} \leq x \leq 1 \end{array} \right.
$$

for all $\theta \in \Theta$ . In this case, we have 

$$
\sigma (\theta) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \{0 \}, & \text {if} 0 <   \theta <   \frac {1}{2} \\ \{\frac {1}{2} \}, & \text {if} \frac {1}{2} \leq \theta \leq 1 \end{array} \right.,
$$

which is obviously not upper hemicontinuous at ${ \frac { 1 } { 2 } } . ^ { 1 1 }$ Conclusion: Lower semicontinuity $o f \ \varphi$ is essential $f o r$ the validity of the Maximum Theorem. 

Given this observation, it may be instructive to find out exactly where we have used the lower semicontinuity of $\varphi$ while proving the Maximum Theorem. We used it in the second paragraph of the proof when saying that 

$^ { 6 6 } \cdots$ But since $( y ^ { m } , \theta ^ { m } )  ( y , \theta )$ and $( x ^ { m } , \theta ^ { m } )  ( x , \theta )$ , the inequality $\varphi ( y , \theta ) > \varphi ( x , \theta )$ and continuity of $\varphi$ force that $\varphi ( y ^ { m } , \theta ^ { m } ) > \varphi ( x ^ { m } , \theta ^ { m } )$ for m large enough. ...” 

Here is a detailed verification of this claim. Choose an $0 < \varepsilon < \varphi ( y , \theta ) - \varphi ( x , \theta )$ and note that upper semicontinuity of $\varphi$ implies that there exists an $M _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { N }$ such that 

$$
\varphi (y, \theta) > \varphi (x, \theta) + \varepsilon \geq \varphi (x ^ {m}, \theta^ {m}) \quad \text { for   all } m \geq M _ {1}.
$$

So $\varphi ( y , \theta ) > \operatorname* { s u p } \{ \varphi ( x ^ { m } , \theta ^ { m } ) : m \in \mathbb { N } \} = : s$ . Now pick any $0 < \varepsilon ^ { \prime } < \varphi ( y , \theta ) - s$ , and note that, by lower semicontinuity of $\varphi ,$ there exists an $M _ { 2 } > 0$ such that 

$$
\varphi (y ^ {m}, \theta^ {m}) \geq \varphi (y, \theta) - \varepsilon^ {\prime} > s \quad \text { for   all } m \geq M _ {2}.
$$

Thus, for any integer $m \geq \operatorname* { m a x } \{ M _ { 1 } , M _ { 2 } \}$ , we have $\varphi ( y ^ { m } , \theta ^ { m } ) > \varphi ( x ^ { m } , \theta ^ { m } )$ 

Here is a simple example that illustrates how useful the Maximum Theorem may prove in economic applications. (We will later encounter more substantial applications of this theorem.) 

E{dpsoh 4. (The Demand Correspondence) Consider an agent whose income is $\iota > 0$ and whose utility function over n-vectors of commodity bundles is $u : \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { n } \longrightarrow \mathbb { R }$ The standard choice problem of this consumer is to 

$$

$$

where $p \in \mathbb { R } _ { + + } ^ { n }$ stands for the price vector in the economy, and $B : \mathbb { R } _ { + + } ^ { n + 1 } \overset { } { \Longrightarrow } \mathbb { R }$ , defined by $( 2 )$ , is the budget correspondence of the consumer. Clearly, the optimum choice of the individual is conditional on the parameter $( p , \iota )$ , and is thus modeled by the correspondence d $: \mathbb { R } _ { + + } ^ { n + 1 } \overset { } { \implies } \mathbb { R }$ defined by 

$$
\mathbf {d} (p, \iota) := \arg \max \left\{u (x): x \in B (p, \iota) \right\}.
$$

$\mathrm { A s }$ you may recall, the correspondence d is called the demand correspondence of the individual. By Weierstrass’ Theorem, it is well-defined. Moreover, since B is continuous (Examples 2 and 3), we can apply the Maximum Theorem to conclude that d is compact-valued, closed, and upper hemicontinuous. Moreover, the indirect utility function $u ^ { * } : \mathbb { R } _ { + + } ^ { n + 1 }  \mathbb { R }$ defined by $u ^ { * } ( p , \iota ) : = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ u ( x ) : x \in B ( p , \iota ) \}$ , is continuous by the same theorem, and is increasing in ι and decreasing in $p$ by Exercise 39 below. Finally, if we further knew that u is strictly quasiconcave, then we could conclude that d is a continuous function. □

## 4 Application: Stationary Dynamic Programming

In contrast to the one we analyzed in Example 4, the optimization problems that arise in economic theory often possess a structure that is inherently dynamic. Such problems are significantly more complex than the static ones in general, and the application of the Maximum Theorem for them may be somewhat indirect. The stationary discounted dynamic programming theory, the elements of which are introduced in this section, provides a very good case in point.<sup>12</sup> 

## 4.1 The Standard Dynamic Programming Problem

Put concretely, the basic problem is to find a sequence $( x ^ { m } )$ that would 

$$
\text {Maximize} \varphi (x ^ {0}, x ^ {1}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} \varphi (x ^ {i}, x ^ {i + 1})\tag{7}
$$

such that 

$$
x ^ {1} \in \Gamma (x ^ {0}) \quad \text { and } \quad x ^ {m + 1} \in \Gamma (x ^ {m}), m = 1, 2, \dots\tag{8}
$$

Here $x ^ { 0 }$ is any element of a given metric space X. While X is called the state space of the problem, $x ^ { 0 }$ is thought of as the initial state of the dynamical system at hand. Γ is any self-correspondence on X that lets one know which states are possible “tomorrow” given the state of the system “today.” It is called the transition correspondence of the problem. A sequence $( x ^ { m } ) \in X ^ { \infty }$ such that $x ^ { 1 } \in \Gamma ( x ^ { 0 } )$ and $\boldsymbol { x } ^ { m + 1 } \in \Gamma ( \boldsymbol { x } ^ { m } )$ for each $m ,$ , is thought of as a feasible plan of action through time, with $x ^ { m }$ acting as the state of the system at period $m + 1$ . The objective function of the optimization problem is defined through the map $\varphi : G r ( \Gamma ) \longrightarrow \overline { { \mathbb { R } } }$ , which is usually referred to as the (one-period) return function. Finally, the parameter δ is any real number in (0, 1), and is called the discount factor. We think of $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { \infty } \delta ^ { i } \varphi ( x ^ { i } , x ^ { i + 1 } )$ as the present value of the stream of returns that obtain every period (starting from “today”) along the feasible plan $( x ^ { m } )$ 

The following postulate is basic. 

Avvxpswlrq (A0). For any feasible plan $( x ^ { m } ) \in X ^ { \infty }$ 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {k} \delta^ {i} \varphi (x ^ {i}, x ^ {i + 1}) \in \overline {{\mathbb {R}}}.
$$

This assumption says that it is possible to compute the present value of the intertemporal stream of returns that is induced by any feasible plan, but it allows for this value to be $- \infty \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } \infty$ . Put diferently, all that (A0) outrules is the possibility of endless oscillations along a feasible plan. In this sense, it can be viewed as a natural hypothesis for the general development of the theory. 

The primitives of the model are then contained in the list $( X , x ^ { 0 } , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta )$ . When it satisfies (A0), we call such list a standard dynamic programming problem. With an innocent abuse of terminology, we will also refer to the associated maximization problem (7)-(8) in the same way. 

Let us now introduce two further assumptions that will play a decisive role in the general development of the theory. Note that the first one of these postulates implies (A0). 

Avvxpswlrq (A1). $\varphi$ is continuous and bounded. 

Avvxpswlrq (A2). Γ is compact-valued and continuous. 

There are many economic problems that can be modeled as standard dynamic programming problems that satisfy (A1) and (A2) — the comprehensive treatment of Stokey and Lucas (1989) provides a good number of concrete examples. 

The first question that we wish to address here is if there exists a solution to a standard dynamic programming problem under the assumptions stated above. Secondly, if the answer is yes (and it is, of course; what did you expect?), we would like to be able to say something about the continuity of the optimal solution(s). 

For any given standard dynamic programming problem $( X , x ^ { 0 } , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta )$ , we define the class 

$$
\mathcal {D} (X, \Gamma , \varphi , \delta) := \{(X, x, \Gamma , \varphi , \delta): x \in X \},\tag{9}
$$

which is the collection of all dynamic programming problems that difer from our original problem only in their initial states. The class of all such collections of standard dynamic programming problems are denoted by $\mathcal { D P }$ 

The basic objects of analysis in dynamic programming are the members of $\mathcal { D P }$ that is, collections of the form (9). The main reason why we work with such collections instead of an arbitrary standard dynamic programming problem with a fixed initial state is the following. Given that we choose, say $x ^ { 1 }$ , in the first period, the optimization problem from the second period onward looks exactly like our original problem except that the initial state of the latter problem is $x ^ { 1 }$ . Put diferently, due to the basic recursive structure of dynamic programming problems, when we look from period m onward, the problem at hand would be none other than $( X , x ^ { m } , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta )$ for any $m \in \mathbb { N }$ . Thus, even though the initial state of the original problem may be fixed, one would still need to develop an understanding of the problem for various choices of initial states. This point will become clearer as we go along. 

Let us try to rewrite our optimization problem in more familiar terms. Let $\Omega _ { \Gamma } ( x )$ stand for the set of all feasible plans for the problem $( X , x , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta )$ . That is, define the correspondence $\Omega _ { \Gamma } : X \supseteq X ^ { \infty }$ by 

$$
\Omega_ {\Gamma} (x) := \{(x ^ {m}) \in X ^ {\infty}: x ^ {1} \in \Gamma (x) \text {and} x ^ {m + 1} \in \Gamma (x ^ {m}), m \in \mathbb {N} \}.
$$

Define next the map $F _ { \Gamma , \varphi } : \{ \Omega _ { \Gamma } ( x ) \times \{ x \} : x \in X \} \to { \overline { { \mathbb { R } } } }$ by 

$$
F _ {\Gamma , \varphi} ((x ^ {m}), x) := \varphi (x, x ^ {1}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} \varphi (x ^ {i}, x ^ {i + 1}).
$$

(Of course $F _ { \Gamma , \varphi }$ depends also on the discount factor $\delta ,$ but we will keep δ fixed throughout the discussion, so there is no need to make this dependence explicit in our notation.) Thanks to (A0), $F _ { \Gamma , \varphi }$ is well-defined, but it may assume the value of $- \infty$ or along a feasible plan. If, however, $\varphi$ satisfies $( \mathrm { A 1 } )$ , then $F _ { \Gamma , \varphi }$ is not only real-valued, but it is also bounded. For, in this case, there exists a $K > 0$ with $| \varphi | \leq K$ , so 

$$
\left| F _ {\Gamma , \varphi} ((x ^ {m}), x) \right| \leq \left| \varphi (x, x ^ {1}) \right| + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} \left| \varphi (x ^ {i}, x ^ {i + 1}) \right| \leq K + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} K = \frac {K}{1 - \delta}
$$

for all $x \in X$ and $( x ^ { m } ) \in \Omega _ { \Gamma } ( x )$ . (Recall Exercise A.45 and Example A.8.[3].) 

We may now rewrite our optimization problem as 

$$
\text { Maximize } F _ {\Gamma , \varphi} ((x ^ {m}), x) \quad \text { such   that } \quad (x ^ {m}) \in \Omega_ {\Gamma} (x),\tag{10}
$$

where the initial state x is considered as a parameter. Very good, this looks like a problem that we can attack with our conventional weapons (Weierstrass’ Theorem, the Maximum Theorem, etc.), at least under the premises of (A1) and (A2). But to be able to do this, we need to first metrize $X ^ { \infty }$ in such a way that the requirements of the Maximum Theorem are met. While something like this can actually be done, such a direct approach turns out to be a poor method for “solving” (10). Instead, there is an alternative, recursive method that would enable us to bring the power of the Maximum Theorem to the fore in a more striking manner. 

## 4.2 The Principle of Optimality

Fix any $\mathcal { D } : = \mathcal { D } ( \boldsymbol { X } , \boldsymbol { \Gamma } , \boldsymbol { \varphi } , \boldsymbol { \delta } ) \in \mathcal { D P }$ . A major ingredient of the recursive method is the function $V : X  { \overline { { \mathbb { R } } } }$ which is defined by 

$$
V (x) := \sup \left\{F _ {\Gamma , \varphi} ((x ^ {m}), x): (x ^ {m}) \in \Omega_ {\Gamma} (x) \right\}.\tag{11}
$$

(We don’t make explicit the dependence of V on Γ and $\varphi$ to simplify the notation.) Clearly, if $F _ { \Gamma , \varphi }$ is bounded, then $V \in \mathbf { B } ( X )$ . (Note. we can replace the $\mathrm { ^ { * } s u p ^ { \mathrm { * } } }$ here with “max” if a solution to (10) exists.) V is called the value function for the collection . Due to the recursive nature of the problems in $\mathcal { D } ,$ this function will play a very important role in the subsequent analysis. For one thing, provided that a solution to (10) exists, we can deduce from V the optimal plan for our problem under quite general circumstances. 

Lemma 1. (Bellman) Let $\mathcal { D } ( X , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta ) \in \mathcal { D P }$ , take any $x ^ { 0 } \in X$ and $( x _ { * } ^ { m } ) \in \Omega _ { \Gamma } ( x ^ { 0 } )$ R and define $V : X  \overline { { \mathbb { R } } } \ b y \ ( 1 1 ) . \ I f \ \backslash ( x ^ { 0 } ) = F _ { \Gamma , \varphi } ( ( x _ { * } ^ { m } ) , x ^ { 0 } )$ , then 

$$
V (x ^ {0}) = \varphi (x ^ {0}, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \delta V (x _ {*} ^ {1}) \quad a n d \quad V (x _ {*} ^ {m}) = \varphi (x _ {*} ^ {m}, x _ {*} ^ {m + 1}) + \delta V (x _ {*} ^ {m + 1})\tag{12}
$$

for each $m = 1 , 2 , \ldots . ^ { 1 3 } \ { \cal I f }$ (A1) holds, the converse is also true. 

Proof. (To simplify the notation, we denote $F _ { \Gamma , \varphi }$ by $F ,$ and $\Omega _ { \Gamma }$ by $\Omega _ { ; }$ , throughout the proof.) By definition, $V ( x ^ { 0 } ) = F ( ( x _ { * } ^ { m } ) , x ^ { 0 } )$ means that 

$$
\varphi (x ^ {0}, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} \varphi (x _ {*} ^ {i}, x _ {*} ^ {i + 1}) \geq \varphi (x ^ {0}, x ^ {1}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} \varphi (x ^ {i}, x ^ {i + 1})
$$

for any $( x ^ { m } ) \in \Omega ( x ^ { 0 } )$ . Since $( x ^ { 2 } , x ^ { 3 } , \ldots ) \in \Omega ( x _ { * } ^ { 1 } )$ implies that $( x _ { * } ^ { 1 } , x ^ { 2 } , x ^ { 3 } , \ldots ) \in \Omega ( x ^ { 0 } )$ (notice the use of the recursive structure here), we then find 

$$
\varphi (x ^ {0}, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} \varphi (x _ {*} ^ {i}, x _ {*} ^ {i + 1}) \geq \varphi (x ^ {0}, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \delta \varphi (x _ {*} ^ {1}, x ^ {2}) + \sum_ {i = 2} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} \varphi (x ^ {i}, x ^ {i + 1}),
$$

that is, $F ( ( x _ { * } ^ { 2 } , x _ { * } ^ { 3 } , . . . ) , x _ { * } ^ { 1 } ) \ \geq \ F ( ( x ^ { 2 } , x ^ { 3 } , . . . ) , x _ { * } ^ { 1 } )$ , for all $( x ^ { 2 } , x ^ { 3 } , \ldots ) \ \in \ \Omega ( x _ { * } ^ { 1 } )$ . Thus, $V ( x _ { * } ^ { 1 } ) = F ( ( x _ { * } ^ { 2 } , x _ { * } ^ { 3 } , . . . ) , x _ { * } ^ { 1 } )$ , and hence 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} V (x ^ {0}) & = & F ((x _ {*} ^ {m}), x ^ {0}) \\ & = & \varphi (x ^ {0}, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \delta \left(\varphi (x _ {*} ^ {1}, x _ {*} ^ {2}) + \sum_ {i = 2} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i - 1} \varphi (x _ {*} ^ {i}, x _ {*} ^ {i + 1})\right) \\ & = & \varphi (x ^ {0}, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \delta F ((x _ {*} ^ {2}, x _ {*} ^ {3}, \ldots), x _ {*} ^ {1}) \\ & = & \varphi (x ^ {0}, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \delta V (x _ {*} ^ {1}). \end{array}
$$

The rest of the claim follows by induction. Conversely, assume that (A1) holds, and let $x ^ { 0 } \in X$ and $( x _ { * } ^ { m } ) \in \Omega ( x ^ { 0 } )$ satisfy (12). Then, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} V (x ^ {0}) & = & \varphi (x ^ {0}, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \delta V (x _ {*} ^ {1}) \\ & = & \varphi (x ^ {0}, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \delta \varphi (x _ {*} ^ {1}, x _ {*} ^ {2}) + \delta^ {2} V (x _ {*} ^ {2}) \\ & = & \dots \\ & = & \varphi (x ^ {0}, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \delta^ {i} \varphi (x _ {*} ^ {i}, x _ {*} ^ {i + 1}) + \delta^ {k + 1} V (x _ {*} ^ {k + 1}) \end{array}
$$

for any $k \in \mathbb N$ . But, thanks to (A1), V is bounded, so there exists a $K > 0$ such that $| V | \leq K$ , and this clearly entails that $\delta ^ { k } V ( x ^ { k } ) \to 0$ . (Right?) Thus, letting $k \to \infty$ we obtain $V ( x ^ { 0 } ) = F ( ( x _ { * } ^ { m } ) , x ^ { 0 } )$ , as we sought.  

Exercise 45. Give an example to show that (A1) cannot be omitted in the statement of Lemma 1. 

The second part of Lemma 1 tells us how to go from the value function V of a standard dynamic programming problem with (A1) to its optimal path, provided that the problem has a solution. Consequently, we define the optimal policy correspondence for $\mathcal { D } ( X , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta ) \in \mathcal { D P }$ as the self-correspondence P on X with 

$$
P (x) := \arg \max \left\{\varphi (x, y) + \delta V (y): y \in \Gamma (x) \right\},
$$

provided that a solution to (10) exists, that is, $V ( x ) = \mathrm { m a x } \{ F _ { \Gamma , \varphi } ( ( x ^ { m } ) , x ) : ( x ^ { m } ) \in$ $\Omega _ { \Gamma } ( x ) \}$ for each $x \in X$ . Thanks to Lemma 1, if (A1) holds and a solution to (10) exists, then $( x ^ { m } ) \in X ^ { \infty }$ is a solution to (10) if $x ^ { 1 } \in P ( x ^ { 0 } ) , x ^ { 2 } \in P ( x ^ { 1 } )$ , and so on. (Really? Does Lemma 1 say all this? Please go slow here.) In turn, we will deal with the existence problem by using the following important result, which is often referred to as the Principle of Optimality. 

Lemma 2. (Bellman) For any $\mathcal { D } ( X , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta ) \in \mathcal { D P }$ and $W \in \mathbf { B } ( X )$ 

$$
W (x) = \max \left\{\varphi (x, y) + \delta W (y): y \in \Gamma (x) \right\} \quad \text { for   all } x \in X,\tag{13}
$$

implies 

$$
W (x) = \max \left\{F _ {\Gamma , \varphi} ((x ^ {m}), x): (x ^ {m}) \in \Omega_ {\Gamma} (x) \right\} \quad \text {   for   all   } x \in X.
$$

So, thanks to this observation, the existence problem at hand becomes one of finding a solution to the functional equation (13). If there is a solution $W$ to (13), then this solution, according to Lemma 2, is the value function for our dynamic programming problem. All this is nice, because we have earlier learned some techniques (in Sections C.6 and $\mathrm { C } . 7 )$ which we can use to “solve” (13). But, no need to rush! Let us first prove the claim at hand. 

Proof of Lemma 2. (To simplify the notation, we again denote $F _ { \Gamma , \varphi }$ by $F ,$ and $\Omega _ { \Gamma }$ by $\Omega ,$ , throughout the proof.) Assume that $W \in \mathbf { B } ( X )$ satisfies (13), and fix an arbitrary $x \in X$ . By (13), for an arbitrarily chosen $( x ^ { m } ) \in \Omega ( x )$ 2 

$$
W (x) \geq \varphi (x, x ^ {1}) + \delta W (x ^ {1}) \geq \varphi (x, x ^ {1}) + \delta \varphi (x ^ {1}, x ^ {2}) + \delta^ {2} W (x ^ {2}) \geq \dots
$$

so, proceeding inductively, 

$$
W (x) \geq \left(\varphi (x, x ^ {1}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \delta^ {i} \varphi (x ^ {i}, x ^ {i + 1})\right) + \delta^ {k + 1} W (x ^ {k + 1}) \quad \text { for   all } k = 1, 2, \dots
$$

Thus, ${ \mathrm { i f ~ } } \sum ^ { \infty } \delta ^ { i } \varphi ( x ^ { i } , x ^ { i + 1 } ) > - \infty \ - \quad$ otherwise $W ( x ) \geq F ( ( x ^ { m } ) , x )$ obtains trivially — letting $k \to \infty$ yields 

$$
W (x) \geq F ((x ^ {m}), x) + \lim _ {k \to \infty} \delta^ {k} W (x ^ {k}).
$$

But since W is bounded by hypothesis, the real sequence $\left( \delta ^ { k } W ( x ^ { k } ) \right)$ converges; indeed we have lim $\delta ^ { k } W ( x ^ { k } ) = 0$ . Conclusion: $W ( x ) \geq F ( ( x ^ { m } ) , x )$ for any $( x ^ { m } ) \in \Omega ( x )$ . (We are not done yet. Why?) 

Now choose a sequence $( x _ { * } ^ { m } )$ in $\Omega ( x )$ such that $W ( x ) = \varphi ( x , x _ { * } ^ { 1 } ) + \delta W ( x _ { * } ^ { 1 } )$ , and 

$$
W (x _ {*} ^ {m}) = \varphi (x _ {*} ^ {m}, x _ {*} ^ {m + 1}) + \delta W (x _ {*} ^ {m + 1}), \quad m = 1, 2, \dots
$$

(By (13) there exists such a sequence.) Thus, for any $k \in \mathbb N$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} W (x) & = & \varphi (x, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \delta \varphi (x _ {*} ^ {1}, x _ {*} ^ {2}) + \dots + \delta^ {k} \varphi (x _ {*} ^ {k}, x _ {*} ^ {k + 1}) + \delta^ {k + 1} W (x _ {*} ^ {k + 1}) \\ & = & \left(\varphi (x, x _ {*} ^ {1}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \delta^ {m} \varphi (x _ {*} ^ {i}, x _ {*} ^ {i + 1})\right) + \delta^ {k + 1} W (x _ {*} ^ {k + 1}). \end{array}
$$

Since W is bounded, letting $k  \infty$ yields $W ( x ) = F ( ( x _ { * } ^ { m } ) , x )$ . Since $( x _ { * } ^ { m } ) \in \Omega ( x )$ 2 combining this with the finding of the previous paragraph completes the proof. 

$$

$$

$$

The following two examples aim to demonstrate the importance of Lemma 2. 

E{dpsoh 5. For any $0 \leq x _ { 0 } \leq 1$ , consider the problem of choosing a real sequence $\left( x _ { m } \right)$ in order to 

$$
\mathrm{Maximize} \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {i}} \ln (\sqrt {x _ {i}} - x _ {i + 1})
$$

such that 

$$
0 \leq x _ {m + 1} \leq \sqrt {x _ {m}}, m = 0, 1, \dots
$$

We may view this problem as a standard dynamic programming problem $( X , x _ { 0 } , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta )$ where $X : = [ 0 , 1 ] , \Gamma ( x ) : = [ 0 , \sqrt { x } ] , \varphi ( x , y ) : = \ln ( \sqrt { x } - y )$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { \delta = \frac { 1 } { 2 } . } \end{array}$ . (Check that (A0) is satisfied.) This problem satisfies neither (A1) nor (A2), but this is okay, since here we will solve it using directly the Principle of Optimality which does not require either of these postulates. 

Our first objective is to compute the value function of the problem. Lemma 2 says that it is suficient to solve the following functional equation for this purpose: 

$$
W (x) = \max \left\{\ln (\sqrt {x} - y) + \frac {1}{2} W (y): 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt {x} \right\}, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 1.\tag{14}
$$

But how do we solve $\mathrm { \ t h i s { ? } ^ { 1 4 } }$ The key observation is that we just need to find one $W \in \mathbf { B } ( X )$ that does the job. Thus if we “guessed” the W right, we would be readily in business. Now, here is a rabbit-out-of-the-hat guess which will work: For some $\alpha \geq 0$ and $\beta \in \mathbb { R } , W ( x ) = \alpha \ln x + \beta$ for all $x \in X . ^ { 1 5 }$ With this guess at hand, the problem is to find an $( \alpha , \beta ) \in \mathbb { R } _ { + } \times \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
\alpha \ln x + \beta = \max \left\{\ln (\sqrt {x} - y) + \frac {\alpha}{2} \ln y + \frac {\beta}{2}: 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt {x} \right\}, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 1.
$$

This is nothing that good old calculus can’t handle: $\textstyle y = { \frac { \alpha } { 2 + \alpha } } { \sqrt { x } }$ solves the associated maximization problem, so 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \alpha \ln x + \beta & = & \ln (\sqrt {x} - \frac {\alpha}{2 + \alpha} \sqrt {x}) + \frac {\alpha}{2} \ln \frac {\alpha}{2 + \alpha} \sqrt {x} + \frac {\beta}{2} \\ & = & \left(\frac {1}{2} + \frac {\alpha}{4}\right) \ln x + \ln \left(1 - \frac {\alpha}{2 + \alpha}\right) + \frac {\alpha}{2} \ln \frac {\alpha}{2 + \alpha} + \frac {\beta}{2} \end{array}
$$

for each $x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ . This, in turn, gives us two equations 

$$
\alpha = \frac {1}{2} + \frac {\alpha}{4} \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \beta = \ln \left(1 - \frac {\alpha}{2 + \alpha}\right) + \frac {\alpha}{2} \ln \frac {\alpha}{2 + \alpha} + \frac {\beta}{2}
$$

which are readily solved to find $\begin{array} { r } { \alpha = \frac { 2 } { 3 } } \end{array}$ and $\beta = \ln 9 - \frac { 8 } { 3 }$ ln 4. Therefore, by Lemma $2 ,$ we may conclude that the value function that we are after is $\begin{array} { r } { V ( x ) = \frac { 2 } { 3 } } \end{array}$ ln x+ln $9 - { \frac { 8 } { 3 } }$ ln 4 for each $0 \leq x \leq 1$ . Furthermore, from strict concavity of V and Lemma 1, it follows that the optimal policy correspondence is single-valued: $\begin{array} { r } { P ( x ) = \{ \frac { 1 } { 4 } \sqrt { x } \} } \end{array}$ for any $0 \leq x \leq 1$ □

Find the optimal policy correspondence and the value function for this problem. 

## 4.3 Existence and Uniqueness of an Optimal Solution

Now that we have seen what the Principle of Optimality can do for us, let’s get back to the theory of dynamic programming. For the general theory, we will make use of both (A1) and (A2). Let us then fix an arbitrary $\mathcal { D } ( X , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta ) \in \mathcal { D P }$ for which (A1) and (A2) hold. With the Maximum Theorem in our arsenal, we can in fact establish the existence of a solution to the functional equation (13) relatively easily. We have studied a powerful method of doing this at some length in Section C.7.1, and the same method will work here perfectly. First define the map $\Phi : { \bf C B } ( X )  \mathbb { R } ^ { X }$ by 

$$
\Phi (W) (x) = \max \left\{\varphi (x, y) + \delta W (y): y \in \Gamma (x) \right\} \quad \text { for   all } x \in X.\tag{15}
$$

By the Maximum Theorem, $\Phi ( W )$ is a continuous function, and since both $\varphi$ and $W$ are bounded, so is $\Phi ( W )$ . Thus, Φ is a self-map on CB(X). Moreover, it is readily checked that $W \geq W ^ { \prime }$ implies $\Phi ( W ) \ge \Phi ( W ^ { \prime } )$ and that $\Phi ( W + \alpha ) = \Phi ( W ) + \delta \alpha$ for all $W , W ^ { \prime } \in \mathbf { C B } ( X )$ and $\alpha \geq 0$ . Thus we can apply Lemma C.3 to conclude that Φ is a contraction. Then, by the Banach Fixed Point Theorem, there exists a unique fixed point of Φ in $\mathbf { C B } ( X )$ , call it $\hat { W }$ . Clearly, $\hat { W }$ satisfies (13), and hence by Lemma $2 ,$ we have 

$$
\hat {W} (x) = \max \left\{F _ {\Gamma , \varphi} ((x ^ {m}), x): (x ^ {m}) \in \Omega_ {\Gamma} (x) \right\} \quad \mathrm{forall} x \in X,
$$

as we sought.<sup>16</sup> This proves that a solution to (10) exists, so we conclude: 

Proposition 6. There exists a solution for any standard dynamic programming problem $( X , x ^ { 0 } , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta )$ that satisfies (A1)-(A2). 

Given that (10) has a solution for each $x \in X$ under the hypotheses (A1) and (A2), we may conclude that, for each $x ^ { 0 } \in X$ , an optimal path $( x _ { * } ^ { m } )$ for the problem $( X , x ^ { 0 } , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta )$ exists and satisfies $x _ { * } ^ { 1 } \in P ( x ^ { 0 } ) , x _ { * } ^ { 2 } \in P ( x _ { * } ^ { 1 } )$ , and so on, where, of course, P is the optimal policy correspondence given by 

$$
P (x) = \arg \max \left\{\varphi (x, y) + \delta V (y): y \in \Gamma (x) \right\} \quad \text { for   all } x \in X\tag{16}
$$

with V being the value function for $\mathcal { D } ( \boldsymbol { X } , \boldsymbol { \Gamma } , \boldsymbol { \varphi } , \delta )$ (or equivalently, as we now know, it being the unique solution of (13) in $\mathbf { C B } ( X ) )$ . Thus, the solution to our problem (10) is given by means of a stationary decision correspondence, which tells us what to choose in a period given the choice of the previous period. Moreover, the Maximum Theorem tells us that P is quite well-behaved in that it is compact-valued and upper hemicontinuous. 

We would also like to say something about the uniqueness of the solution to (10), that is, about when P is single-valued. Of course, we need some additional assumptions for this purpose. (Why of course?) To this end, we let X be a nonempty convex set in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n } , n \in \mathbb { N }$ , and posit further regularity properties.<sup>17</sup> 

Avvxpswlrq (A3). Gr(Γ) is convex, that is, for all $0 \leq \lambda \leq 1$ and $x , x ^ { \prime } \in X$ 2 

$$
y \in \Gamma (x) \text {and} y ^ {\prime} \in \Gamma (x ^ {\prime}) \quad \text {imply} \quad \lambda y + (1 - \lambda) y ^ {\prime} \in \Gamma (\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) x ^ {\prime}).
$$

Moreover, $\varphi$ is concave on $G r ( \Gamma )$ , and 

$$
\varphi (\lambda (x, y) + (1 - \lambda) (x ^ {\prime}, y ^ {\prime})) > \lambda \varphi (x, y) + (1 - \lambda) \varphi (x ^ {\prime}, y ^ {\prime})
$$

for all $0 < \lambda < 1$ and $( x , y ) , ( x ^ { \prime } , y ^ { \prime } ) \in G r ( \Gamma )$ with $x \neq x ^ { \prime }$ 

We note that this postulate does not ask for the strict concavity of $\varphi$ on its entire domain. For instance, where Γ is a self-correspondence on [0, 1] with $\Gamma ( x ) : = [ 0 , 1 ]$ for all $0 \leq x \leq 1$ , the map $\varphi : G r ( \Gamma ) \to \mathbb { R }$ defined by $\varphi ( x , y ) : = { \sqrt { x } } - y$ satisfies (A3), but it is not strictly concave on $[ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 }$ 

Now to prove the uniqueness of the solution to (10), we need to show that $P$ is single-valued, and a suficient condition for this is that the unique function in CB(X) that satisfies (13) (i.e. the unique fixed point of Φ) be strictly concave. (Why?) Recall that, by Lemma 2 and the proof of the Banach Fixed Point Theorem, we have lim $\Phi ^ { m } ( W ) = V$ for any choice of W in CB(X). But then if we can prove that Φ maps concave functions to concave functions, then it would follow that $V$ must be concave. (Proof. Pick any concave $W \in \mathbf { C B } ( X )$ and use this claim along with the fact that the uniform (indeed, pointwise) limit of concave functions is concave (Exercise A.67).) So take any $0 < \lambda < 1$ and $x , x ^ { \prime } \in X$ , and note that, by the first part of (A3), 

$$
\Phi (W) (\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) x ^ {\prime}) \geq \varphi (\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) x ^ {\prime}, \lambda y + (1 - \lambda) y ^ {\prime}) + \delta W (\lambda y + (1 - \lambda) y ^ {\prime})
$$

where $y \in P ( x )$ and $y ^ { \prime } \in P ( x ^ { \prime } )$ with P as defined in (16). Then, by concavity of $\varphi$ and W, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \Phi (W) (\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) x ^ {\prime}) & \geq & \lambda (\varphi (x, y) + \delta W (y)) + (1 - \lambda) (\varphi (x ^ {\prime}, y ^ {\prime}) + \delta W (y ^ {\prime})) \\ & \geq & \lambda \Phi (W) (x) + (1 - \lambda) \Phi (W) (x ^ {\prime}), \end{array}
$$

which proves that $\Phi ( W )$ is concave. By using the reasoning noted above, then, we may conclude that V is a concave function. But then we may repeat this analysis with V playing the role of $W ,$ and with $x \neq x ^ { \prime }$ and $0 < \lambda < 1$ , to get 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} V (\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) x ^ {\prime}) & = & \Phi (V) (\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) x ^ {\prime}) \\ & > & \lambda \Phi (V) (x) + (1 - \lambda) \Phi (V) (x ^ {\prime}) \\ & = & \lambda V (x) + (1 - \lambda) V (x ^ {\prime}) \end{array}
$$

by using the second part of (A3). Thus, V must be a strictly concave function. As noted above, this proves: 

Proposition 7. Let X be a nonempty convex subset of a Euclidean space. A standard dynamic programming problem $( X , x ^ { 0 } , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta )$ that satisfies $( \mathrm { A 1 } ) – ( \mathrm { A 3 } )$ has a unique solution. 

Exercise $ 4 9 .$ . Consider a standard dynamic programming problem $( X , x ^ { 0 } , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta )$ that satisfies (A1) and (A2). Assume further that, for any $y \in X$ such that $( x , y ) \in$ $G r ( \Gamma )$ for some $x \in X$ , the map $\varphi ( \cdot , y )$ is strictly increasing (on $\{ x \in X : y \in$ $\Gamma ( x ) \}$ , and that $\Gamma ( x ) \subseteq \Gamma ( x ^ { \prime } )$ whenever $x \leq x ^ { \prime }$ . Prove that the value function of the problem is strictly increasing. 

The following definition introduces a useful concept that often plays an important role in problems that concern the monotonicity of a solution to an optimization problem. 

Dhilqlwlrq. Let $S$ be any nonempty set in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ . A function $f \in \mathbb { R } ^ { S }$ is said to be supermodular on S if 

$$
f (a, b) + f \left(a ^ {\prime}, b ^ {\prime}\right) \geq f \left(a ^ {\prime}, b\right) + f \left(a, b ^ {\prime}\right)
$$

whenever $( a , b ) , ( a ^ { \prime } , b ^ { \prime } ) , ( a , b ^ { \prime } ) , ( a , b ^ { \prime } ) \in S$ and $( a ^ { \prime } , b ^ { \prime } ) \geq ( a , b )$ . If $( a , b )$ and $( a ^ { \prime } , b ^ { \prime } )$ are distinct, and each $\geq$ are replaced with > here, then we say that f is strictly supermodular. 

Exercise 50. Let $\varnothing \neq X \subseteq \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ and consider a standard dynamic programming problem $( X , x _ { 0 } , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta )$ that satisfies $( \mathrm { A 1 } )$ and (A2). Assume: 

(i) $x ^ { \prime } \geq x , y \geq y ^ { \prime }$ and $y \in \Gamma ( x )$ imply $y ^ { \prime } \in \Gamma ( x ^ { \prime } )$ ; 

(ii) $\varphi$ is strictly supermodular on $\mathrm { G r } ( \Gamma )$ 

(a) Let P be the optimal policy correspondence for $\mathcal { D } ( \boldsymbol { X } , \boldsymbol { \Gamma } , \boldsymbol { \varphi } , \delta )$ . Prove that if the self-map p on $X$ is a selection from $P ,$ that is, $p ( x ) \in P ( x )$ for all $x \in X$ , then $p$ must be an increasing function.<sup>18</sup> 

(b) (A Turnpike Theorem) Show that if X is compact, then for each optimal path $( x _ { m } ^ { * } )$ for $( X , x _ { 0 } , \Gamma , \varphi , \delta )$ there exists an $x \in X$ such that $x _ { m } ^ { * } \to x \in P ( x )$ 

By positing further properties on the primitives of a standard dynamic programming problem, one may say more about the structure of the optimal policy and value functions. We shall, however, stop our discussion at this point noting that three excellent references to further your knowledge about this important topic is Bertsekas (1976), Stokey and Lucas (1989) and Mitra (2000).<sup>19</sup> 

We turn now to a somewhat detailed analysis of an economic model by using the ideas introduced above. For other important economic applications we can do no better than referring you again to Stokey and Lucas (1989) and Ljungqvist and Sargent (2004). 

## 4.4 Application: The Optimal Growth Model

The primitives of the (one-sector) optimal growth model is the initial capital stock $x _ { 0 } > 0$ , the discount factor $0 < \delta < 1$ , the production function $F : \mathbb { R } _ { + } \stackrel { } { \longrightarrow } \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ , and the (social) utility function $u : \mathbb { R } _ { + } \to$ R. With these givens the optimization problem of the model is to 

$$
\mathrm{Maximize} \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} u (F (x _ {i}) - x _ {i + 1})\tag{17}
$$

such that 

$$
0 \leq x _ {m + 1} \leq F (x _ {m}), m = 0, 1, \dots ,\tag{18}
$$

where the maximization is over the sequence of investment levels $\left( x _ { m } \right)$ . The idea is that there is a single good which may be consumed or invested at every period m. An investment of $x _ { m + 1 }$ at period m yields a return of $F ( x _ { m + 1 } )$ at period $m + 1$ . Thus at period m, the level of consumption is $F ( x _ { m } ) - x _ { m + 1 }$ yielding for the social planner, a utility level of $u ( F ( x _ { m } ) - x _ { m + 1 } )$ . The problem of the planner is to choose a capital accumulation plan in order to maximize the discounted sum of the stream of utilities. In what follows, we will work with the following properties. 

Avvxpswlrq (B). (l) u is a bounded and twice diferentiable function with $u _ { + } ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) =$ $\infty , u ^ { \prime } > 0$ and $u ^ { \prime \prime } < 0$ 

(ll) F is a bounded and twice diferentiable function with $F ( 0 ) = 0 , F _ { + } ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) = \infty$ 2 $F ^ { \prime } > 0$ and $F ^ { \prime \prime } < 0$ 

The list $( x _ { 0 } , F , u , \delta )$ (along with the maximization problem (17)-(18)) is called an optimal growth model, provided that u and F satisfy (B). This model induces a standard dynamic programming problem in a natural manner. If we define $\Gamma _ { F }$ $\mathbb { R } _ { + } \overset { \vartriangle } { \Longrightarrow } \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ by $\Gamma _ { F } ( x ) : = [ 0 , F ( x ) ]$ , and $\varphi _ { u , F } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { G r ( \Gamma ) }$ by $\varphi _ { u , F } ( x , y ) : = u ( F ( x ) - y )$ , then $( \mathbb { R } _ { + } , x _ { 0 } , \Gamma _ { F } , \varphi _ { u , F } , \delta )$ is a standard dynamic programming problem, and the problem (17)-(18) is: 

$$
\mathrm{Maximize} \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} \varphi_ {u, F} (x _ {i}, x _ {i + 1})
$$

such that 

$$
x _ {m + 1} \in \Gamma_ {F} (x _ {m}), m = 0, 1, \dots .
$$

Clearly, $\Gamma _ { F }$ is compact-valued. It is also continuous, thanks to the continuity of F (Exercise 27). Moreover, $\varphi _ { u , F }$ is continuous since so are u and F, and it is bounded since so is u. We may thus apply Proposition 6 to conclude that there exists a solution to the maximization problem (17)-(18) under the premises of (B). Consequently, the value function V for $\mathcal { D } ( \mathbb { R } _ { + } , \Gamma _ { F } , \varphi _ { u , F } , \delta )$ is well-defined, and corresponds to the unique fixed point of the map $\Phi : { \bf C B } ( \mathbb { R } _ { + } )  \mathbb { R } ^ { \mathbb { R } _ { + } }$ defined by (15) (with $\Gamma _ { F }$ and $\varphi _ { u , F }$ playing the roles of Γ and $\varphi ,$ respectively). Thus, we have 

$$
V (x) = \max \left\{u (F (x) - y) + \delta V (y): 0 \leq y \leq F (x) \right\} \quad \text { for   all } x \in \mathbb {R} _ {+}.\tag{19}
$$

Given that u and $F$ are strictly increasing, we may use Exercise 49 to show that this function is strictly increasing. It is also easy to show that $\varphi _ { u , F }$ and $\Gamma _ { F }$ satisfy (A3). For instance, $\varphi _ { u , F }$ is concave, because, for any $( x , y ) , ( x ^ { \prime } , y ^ { \prime } ) \in G r ( \Gamma _ { F } )$ and $0 \leq \lambda \leq 1$ ， 

$$
\begin{array}{l l l} \varphi_ {u, F} (\lambda (x, y) + (1 - \lambda) (x ^ {\prime}, y ^ {\prime})) & = & u (F (\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) x ^ {\prime}) - (\lambda y + (1 - \lambda) y ^ {\prime})) \\ & \geq & u (\lambda (F (x) - y) + (1 - \lambda) (F (x ^ {\prime}) - y ^ {\prime})) \\ & \geq & \lambda u (F (x) - y) + (1 - \lambda) u (F (x ^ {\prime}) - y ^ {\prime}) \\ & = & \lambda \varphi_ {u, F} (x, y) + (1 - \lambda) \varphi_ {u, F} (x ^ {\prime}, y ^ {\prime}) \end{array}
$$

where the first inequality follows from concavity of $F$ and monotonicity of $u ,$ and the second from concavity of $u .$ In view of the discussion preceding Proposition $^ { 7 , }$ therefore, we reach the following conclusion. 

Observation 1. For any optimal growth model there is a unique solution. Moreover, the value function for the associated dynamic programming problem is strictly increasing and strictly concave. 

Consequently, for any optimal growth model $( x _ { 0 } , F , u , \delta )$ , the optimal policy correspondence for $\mathcal { D } ( \mathbb { R } _ { + } , \Gamma _ { F } , \varphi _ { u , F } , \delta )$ can be thought of as a self-map $P$ on $\mathbb { R } _ { + }$ with 

$$
P (x) \in \arg \max \left\{u (F (x) - y) + \delta V (y): 0 \leq y \leq F (x) \right\}.
$$

(This map is called the optimal policy function for $( x _ { 0 } , F , u , \delta ) . )$ In words, $P ( x )$ is the optimal level of savings (investment) at any period with capital stock $x .$ . By the Maximum Theorem, $P$ is a continuous function. Moreover, given the special structure of the optimal growth model, we have the following. 

Observation 2. The optimal policy function $P$ for any optimal growth model $( x _ { 0 } , F _ { \mathrm { { ; } } }$ $u , \delta )$ is increasing. 

Proof. Take any x, $x ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ with $x ^ { \prime } > x$ , and assume that $y : = P ( x ) > P ( x ^ { \prime } ) = : y ^ { \prime }$ By definition of $P$ and (19), we have 

$$
u (F (x) - y) + \delta V (y) \geq u (F (x) - y ^ {\prime}) + \delta V (y ^ {\prime})
$$

since $y ^ { \prime } < y \leq F ( x )$ , and 

$$
u (F (x ^ {\prime}) - y ^ {\prime}) + \delta V (y ^ {\prime}) \geq u (F (x ^ {\prime}) - y) + \delta V (y)
$$

since $y \le F ( x ) \le F ( x ^ { \prime } )$ . Thus, 

$$
u (F (x ^ {\prime}) - y ^ {\prime}) - u (F (x ^ {\prime}) - y) \geq \delta (V (y) - V (y ^ {\prime})) \geq u (F (x) - y ^ {\prime}) - u (F (x) - y)
$$

which is impossible in view of the strict concavity of $u . \mathrm { ( W h y ? ) }$ 

This observation tells us that the optimal investment plan 

$$
(x _ {1} ^ {*}, x _ {2} ^ {*}, \dots) := (P (x _ {0}), P (x _ {1} ^ {*}), \dots)
$$

for any optimal growth model $( x _ { 0 } , F , u , \delta )$ is monotonic. Indeed, if $x _ { 1 } ^ { * } \geq x _ { 0 }$ , then $x _ { 2 } ^ { * } = P ( x _ { 1 } ^ { * } ) \geq P ( x ^ { 0 } ) = x _ { 1 } ^ { * }$ and so on, that is, in this case the optimal plan has it that one invests more and more every period. $\operatorname { I f } ,$ on the other hand, $x _ { 1 } ^ { * } < x _ { 0 }$ , then the analogous reasoning shows that the optimal plan must be a decreasing sequence. Thus, the optimal investment plan cannot have any cycles — it is a monotonic sequence in $\mathbb { R } _ { + }$ . In particular, it converges to some point of $\overline { { \mathbb { R } } } _ { + }$ (Proposition A.8). 

What can we say about the limit of $( x _ { m } ^ { * } ) ?$ Answering this question becomes relatively easy once it is observed that, for each $x \geq 0$ , 

$$
P (x) \in \arg \max \left\{u (F (x) - y) + \delta u (F (y) - P (P (x))) + \delta^ {2} V (P (P (x))), 0 \leq y \leq F (x) \right\}
$$

which is an instance of the so-called one-deviation property. (Now this is a serious step. It is best if you struggle with this yourself, and see why P must satisfy this property. So take a deep breath, and try to see why $( P ( x ) , P ( P ( x ) ) , . . . )$ would not be optimal if the assertion above failed. Once you see this, the rest is a walk in the park.) Since everything is diferentiable here, and since the solution of the associated optimization problem must be interior, thanks to the boundary conditions $u _ { + } ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) =$ $F _ { + } ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) = \infty$ , we must have 

$$
u ^ {\prime} (F (x) - P (x)) = \delta u ^ {\prime} \left(F (P (x)) - P (P (x))\right) F ^ {\prime} (P (x))
$$

which is called the Ramsey-Euler equation. This recursive equation is really all that we need to know about the optimal plans of consumption and investment in the present model. Let us denote by $( c _ { m } ^ { * } )$ the optimal consumption plan for $( x _ { 0 } , F , u , \delta )$ , that is, $( c _ { m } ^ { * } ) : = ( F ( x _ { 0 } ) - x _ { 1 } ^ { * } , F ( x _ { 1 } ^ { * } ) - x _ { 2 } ^ { * } , \ldots )$ . The Ramsey-Euler equation then yields 

$$
u ^ {\prime} (c _ {m} ^ {*}) = \delta u ^ {\prime} (c _ {m + 1} ^ {*}) F ^ {\prime} (x _ {m} ^ {*}), \quad m = 1, 2, \dots\tag{20}
$$

We leave it to you to show that this equation and the strict concavity of u entail that $\left( c _ { m } ^ { * } \right)$ is a monotonic, and hence convergent, sequence. (Don’t forget that we do not know if P is diferentiable when proving this claim.) Since $F$ is bounded, $c _ { m } ^ { * } \to \infty$ is impossible, so we have lim $c _ { m } ^ { * } \in \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ 

By a steady-state of the model $( x _ { 0 } , F , u , \delta )$ , we mean a level of capital stock x in which the level of investment (and hence consumption) stays the same throughout all periods: $x = P ( x )$ . From the Ramsey-Euler equation and the strict concavity of $F$ it follows that there is a unique steady-state of the model, call it $x ^ { G }$ , which is characterized by $\begin{array} { r } { F ^ { \prime } ( x ^ { G } ) = \frac { 1 } { \delta } } \end{array}$ . (Surprisingly, $x ^ { G }$ depends only on $F$ and $\delta . )$ In the literature on growth theory $x ^ { G }$ is referred to as the golden-rule level of investment. The main reason for choosing such a flashy name is given by the final result of this section. 

Observation 3. (Turnpike Theorem) The optimal investment and consumption plans $( x _ { m } ^ { * } )$ and $( c _ { m } ^ { * } )$ for any given optimal growth model $( x _ { 0 } , F , u , \delta )$ are monotonic sequences with 

$$
\lim _ {m \to \infty} x _ {m} ^ {*} = x ^ {G} \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \lim _ {m \to \infty} c _ {m} ^ {*} = F (x ^ {G}) - x ^ {G},
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { F ^ { \prime } ( x ^ { G } ) = \frac { 1 } { \delta } } \end{array}$ 

Proof. The monotonicity (hence convergence) claims were already verified above. Letting now $m \to \infty$ in (20) and using the continuity of $u ^ { \prime }$ and $F ^ { \prime }$ , we find $u ^ { \prime } ( \operatorname* { l i m } c _ { m } ^ { * } ) =$ $\delta u ^ { \prime } ( \operatorname* { l i m } c _ { m } ^ { * } ) F ^ { \prime } ( \operatorname* { l i m } x _ { m } ^ { * } )$ which yields $\begin{array} { r } { F ^ { \prime } ( \operatorname* { l i m } x _ { m } ^ { * } ) ~ = ~ \frac { 1 } { \delta } ~ = ~ F ^ { \prime } ( x ^ { G } ) } \end{array}$ . Thus, since $F ^ { \prime }$ strictly decreasing, lim $x _ { m } ^ { * } = x ^ { G }$ . That lim $c _ { m } ^ { * } = \check { F ( x ^ { G } ) } - x ^ { G }$ then follows readily from the continuity of $F .$ □ 

This is a truly remarkable result. It tells us that regardless of the initial capital stock and the (per period) utility function, the optimal investment policy tends through time to a fixed level $x ^ { G }$ 

We conclude with a few exercises from intertemporal economics, the analyses of which parallel closely the one sketched above for the optimal growth model.

\frac {v ^ {\prime} (a)}{v ^ {\prime} (b)} \geq \frac {\beta}{\alpha} \frac {u ^ {\prime} (a)}{u ^ {\prime} (b)} \quad \mathrm{forany} a, b \geq 0,
$$

then $x _ { m } \geq y _ { m }$ for all $m = 1 , 2 , \ldots$ (Interpretation. In the one-sector optimal growth model, the optimal capital stock of a country can never fall strictly below that of a more delay averse country.)

Denote the value function for $\mathcal { D } ( \mathbb { R } _ { + } , \Gamma _ { F } , \varphi _ { u , F } , \delta )$ by $V ( \cdot , \delta )$ , and the optimal policy function for $( x _ { 0 } , F , u , \delta )$ by $P ( \cdot , \delta )$ , making the dependence of these maps on the discount factor δ explicit. ## 5 Fixed Point Theory III

In this section we extend our work on fixed point theory to the context of correspondences. Our main objective in this regard is to derive Kakutani’s famous generalization of the Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem, which is indeed widely applied in economic analysis. However, our approach is slightly indirect in this regard, for we wish to do some sight-seeing on the way, and talk about a few interesting properties of continuous correspondences that are of independent interest. Towards the end of the section, we will also talk about how one may carry the basic idea behind the Banach Fixed Point Theorem to the realm of correspondences. 

## 5.1 Kakutani’s Fixed Point Theorem

The following is one of the most important theorems that are contained in this book. It is also commonly used in economic theory — chances are you have already encountered this result elsewhere. It was proved by Shizuo Kakutani in 1941.<sup>20</sup> 

Kakutani’s Fixed Point Theorem. For any given $n \in \mathbb N$ , let X be a nonempty, closed, bounded and convex subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . If Γ is a convex-valued self-correspondence on X that has a closed graph, then Γ has a fixed point, that is, there exists an $x \in X$ with $x \in \Gamma ( x )$ 

Exercise 56. (a) Give an example of a convex-valued self-correspondence Γ on [0, 1] which does not have a fixed point. 

(b) Give an example of a closed-valued and upper hemicontinuous self-correspondence Γ on [0, 1] which does not have a fixed point. 

Warning. The requirement of the closed graph property in the statement of Kakutani’s Fixed Point Theorem can be replaced with upper hemicontinuity when Γ is closed-valued. (This is an immediate consequence of Proposition 3.(b).) 

Kakutani’s Fixed Point Theorem generalizes the Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem in a straightforward way. It is thus not surprising that this result finds wide applicability in the theory of games and competitive equilibrium. We will actually provide one such application in the next section. For the time being, we ofer the following example to illustrate the typical usage of Kakutani’s Fixed Point Theorem in practice. 

E{dpsoh 6. Let $\varphi$ and $\psi$ be continuous functions on $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ such that, for all $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ (i) $\varphi ( \cdot , x _ { 2 } )$ is quasiconcave and $\psi ( x _ { 1 } , \cdot )$ is quasiconvex; and 

(ii) $\varphi ( [ 0 , 1 ] , x _ { 2 } ) \cap \mathbb { R } _ { + } \neq \varnothing$ and $\psi ( x _ { 1 } , [ 0 , 1 ] ) \cap \mathbb { R } _ { - } \neq \emptyset$ 

We claim that, under these conditions, there exists an $x \in [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 }$ such that 

$$
\varphi (x) \geq 0 \geq \psi (x).
$$

Let us first express this claim as a fixed point problem. Define the self-correspondence $\Gamma _ { \varphi }$ and $\Gamma _ { \psi }$ on [0, 1] by 

$$
\Gamma_ {\varphi} (x _ {2}) := \{a \in [ 0, 1 ]: \varphi (a, x _ {2}) \geq 0 \} \quad \text { and } \quad \Gamma_ {\psi} (x _ {1}) := \{b \in [ 0, 1 ]: \psi (x _ {1}, b) \leq 0 \}.
$$

By (ii), these correspondences are well-defined. Finally, define the self-correspondence Γ on $[ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 }$ by $\Gamma ( x ) : = \Gamma _ { \varphi } ( x _ { 2 } ) \times \Gamma _ { \psi } ( x _ { 1 } )$ . The upshot is that, for any $x \in [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 }$ , we have $x \in \Gamma ( x )$ if $\varphi ( x ) \geq 0 \geq \psi ( x )$ . This is the smart step in the proof, the rest is routine. 

Continuity of $\varphi$ and $\psi$ is easily seen to entail that Γ has a closed graph. Moreover, Γ is convex-valued. Indeed, if $y , z \in \Gamma ( x )$ for any given $x \in [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 }$ , then by quasiconcavity of $\varphi ( \cdot , x _ { 2 } )$ , 

$$
\varphi (\lambda y _ {1} + (1 - \lambda) z _ {1}, x _ {2}) \geq \min \{\varphi (y _ {1}, x _ {2}), \varphi (z _ {1}, x _ {2}) \} \geq 0,
$$

and similarly $\psi ( x _ { 1 } , \lambda y _ { 2 } + ( 1 - \lambda ) z _ { 2 } ) \le 0$ , that is, $\lambda y + ( 1 - \lambda ) z \in \Gamma ( x )$ , for all $0 \leq \lambda \leq 1$ Consequently, we may apply Kakutani’s Fixed Point Theorem to find an $x \in [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 }$ with $x \in \Gamma ( x )$ . By definition of Γ, we have $\varphi ( x ) \geq 0 \geq \psi ( x )$ □ 

Some other applications of Kakutani’s Fixed Point Theorem are given in the following set of exercises. 

Exercise $5 7 . ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ For any given $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , let $S$ be a nonempty, closed, bounded and convex subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 n }$ such that if $( x , y ) \in S$ for some $x , y \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , then $( y , z ) \in S$ for some $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . Prove that $( x ^ { \ast } , x ^ { \ast } ) \in S$ for some $x ^ { * } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ 

Exercise $5 8 . ^ { \mathrm { H } } \operatorname { L e t } X$ be a nonempty, closed, bounded and convex subset of a Euclidean space. Prove: If $\varphi \in \mathbf { C } ( X ^ { 2 } )$ is such that $\varphi ( x , \cdot )$ is quasiconcave for any (fixed) $x \in X$ , then there exists an $x ^ { * } \in X$ with 

$$
\varphi (x ^ {*}, x ^ {*}) = \max \{\varphi (x ^ {*}, y): y \in X \}.
$$

Exercise $5 9 . ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ (The Minimax Theorem) Let X and Y be nonempty, closed, bounded and convex subsets of any two Euclidean spaces. Prove that if $\varphi \in \mathbb { R } ^ { X \times Y }$ is continuous, and if the sets $\left\{ z \in X : \varphi ( z , y ) \geq \alpha \right\}$ and $\{ w \in Y : \varphi ( x , w ) \leq \alpha \}$ are convex for each $( x , y , \alpha ) \in X \times Y \times \mathbb { R }$ , then

\max \{\{\min \varphi (x, y): y \in Y \}: x \in X \} = \min \{\{\max \varphi (x, y): x \in X \}: y \in Y \}.
$$

Exercise $6 0 . ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ Given a nonempty, closed, bounded and convex subset X of a Euclidean space, let $f$ be a continuous self-map on X, and Γ a convex-valued self-correspondence on $X$ with a closed graph. Prove: If $f ( \Gamma ( x ) ) = \Gamma ( f ( x ) )$ for any $x \in X$ , then there is a common fixed point of $f$ and Γ, that is, $f ( x ^ { * } ) = x ^ { * } \in \Gamma ( x ^ { * } )$ for some $x ^ { * } \in X$ 

## 5.2 Michael’s Selection Theorem

Our main objective now is to ofer a proof of Kakutani’s Fixed Point Theorem, which is based on the Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem.<sup>21</sup> While doing this, we will also encounter a number of important results about correspondences which are of independent interest. In particular, in this subsection we will investigate when one may be able to “select” a continuous function from a given correspondence. 

Let us begin by noting the following useful strengthening of Urysohn’s Lemma (Section D.7). 

Lemma 3. (Partition of $U n i t y )$ For any given positive integer $k ,$ , let X be a metric space, and $\{ O _ { 1 } , . . . , O _ { k } \}$ an open cover of X. Then, there exist continuous functions $\varphi _ { 1 } , . . . , \varphi _ { k }$ in $[ 0 , 1 ] ^ { X }$ such that 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \varphi_ {i} = 1 \quad \text { and } \quad \varphi_ {i} | _ {X \setminus O _ {i}} = 0, i = 1,..., k.
$$

Proof. It is without loss of generality to assume that each $O _ { i }$ is nonempty. Moreover, if $O _ { i } = X$ for some i, then we are done by setting $\varphi _ { i } = 1$ and $\varphi _ { j } = 0$ for all $j \neq i$ . Then, assume that each $O _ { i }$ is a nonempty proper subset of $X ,$ , and define $\vartheta _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { X }$ by $\vartheta _ { i } ( x ) : = d ( x , X \backslash O _ { i } ) , i = 1 , . . . , k$ . By Example D.1.[3], each $\vartheta _ { i }$ is continuous on X, and obviously, $\vartheta _ { i } \vert _ { X \backslash O _ { i } } = 0$ for each i. Moreover, it is impossible that $\vartheta _ { 1 } ( x ) = \cdot \cdot \cdot = \vartheta _ { k } ( x ) = 0$ for some $x \in X$ , for in view of Exercise $\mathrm { D . 2 . ( a ) }$ , this would mean that x lies outside of each $O _ { i } ,$ , contradicting that $\{ O _ { 1 } , . . . , O _ { k } \}$ covers X. We may thus define $\varphi _ { j } \in [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { X }$ by $\varphi _ { j } : = \vartheta _ { j } / \sum ^ { k } \vartheta _ { i } , j = 1 , . . . , k$ , to obtain the desired set of functions. 

Urysohn’s Lemma is an immediate consequence of Lemma 3. Indeed, if A and $B$ are nonempty disjoint closed sets in a metric space $X ,$ then $\{ X \backslash A , X \backslash B \}$ is an open cover of $X ,$ so it follows from Lemma 3 that there exist $\psi , \varphi \in \mathbf { C } ( X )$ with $\psi + \varphi = 1$ and $\psi | _ { X \backslash A } = 0 = \varphi | _ { X \backslash B }$ . Thus $\varphi | _ { A } = 0$ and $\varphi | _ { B } = 1$ , that is, ϕ satisfies the requirements of Urysohn’s Lemma.<sup>22</sup> 

Recall that, for any given metric space T and positive integer $n , \mathbf { C } ( T , \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ stands for the set of all continuous functions from T into $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . Moreover, we metrize this set by the sup-metric (Exercise D.45). Here is the main implication we wish to draw from Lemma 3. 

The Approximate Selection Lemma. (Cellina) For any given $n \in \mathbb { N } .$ let X be a nonempty, closed, bounded and convex subset of R<sup>n</sup>, and $\Psi : X  \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ a convexvalued and lower hemicontinuous correspondence. Then, for $\mathrm { a n y } \ \varepsilon > 0$ , there exists a $\varphi \in \mathbf { C } ( X , \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ such that 

$$
d _ {2} (\varphi (x), \Psi (x)) <   \varepsilon \quad \text {   for   each   } x \in X.
$$

Moreover, if Ψ is a self-correspondence, $\varphi$ can be chosen as a self-map. 

Proof. For any $y \in \Psi ( X )$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ , define 

$$
O (y) := \{x \in X: d _ {2} (y, \Psi (x)) <   \frac {\varepsilon}{2} \}.
$$

The lower hemicontinuity of Ψ ensures that this set is open. (Verify!) So $\{ O ( y ) : y \in$ $\mathbb { R } ^ { n } \}$ is an open cover of X, and by compactness of X (Theorem C.1), we can find finitely many $y ^ { 1 } , . . . , y ^ { k }$ in $\Psi ( X )$ such that $\{ O ( y ^ { i } ) : i = 1 , . . . , k \}$ covers X. By Lemma 3, then, there exist continuous functions $\varphi _ { 1 } , . . . , \varphi _ { k }$ in $[ 0 , 1 ] ^ { X }$ such that $\sum ^ { k } \varphi _ { i } = 1$ and $\varphi _ { i } ( x ) = 0$ whenever $x \in X \backslash O ( y ^ { i } ) , i = 1 , . . . , k$ . We define $\varphi : X \to \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ by $\varphi ( x ) : =$ $\sum ^ { k } \varphi _ { i } ( x ) y ^ { i }$ . This function is continuous, because each $\varphi _ { i }$ is continuous. Now take an arbitrary $x \in X$ , and let $I ( x ) : = \{ i : x \in O ( y ^ { i } ) \}$ . Obviously, $\begin{array} { r } { \varphi ( x ) : = \sum _ { i \in I ( x ) } \varphi _ { i } ( x ) y ^ { i } } \end{array}$ (and $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i \in I ( x ) } \varphi _ { i } ( x ) = 1 ) } \end{array}$ . Moreover, for each $i \in I ( x )$ , we have $d _ { 2 } ( y ^ { i } , \Psi ( x ) ) < \frac { \varepsilon } { 2 }$ , so $d _ { 2 } ( y ^ { i } , z ^ { i } ) < \varepsilon$ for some $z ^ { i } \in \Psi ( x )$ . Let $\begin{array} { r } { z : = \sum _ { i \in I ( x ) } \varphi _ { i } ( x ) z ^ { i } } \end{array}$ and notice that $z \in \Psi ( x )$ since $\Psi ( x )$ is convex. But then, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} d _ {2} \left(\varphi (x), z\right) & = & d _ {2} \left(\sum_ {i \in I (x)} \varphi_ {i} (x) y ^ {i}, \sum_ {i \in I (x)} \varphi_ {i} (x) z ^ {i}\right) \\ & \leq & \sum_ {i \in I (x)} \varphi_ {i} (x) d _ {2} \left(y ^ {i}, z ^ {i}\right) \\ & <   & \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

(Why the first inequality?) Thus $d _ { 2 } ( \varphi ( x ) , \Psi ( x ) ) < \varepsilon .$ , and hence the first assertion of the lemma. The second assertion follows readily, because $\Psi ( X ) \subseteq X$ and convexity of X ensure that $\varphi ( x ) \in X$ for each $x \in X$  

It is important to note that lower hemicontinuity is quite essential here. We cannot even replace it with upper hemicontinuity. For instance, the correspondence 

$$
\Psi (x) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \{0 \}, & 0 \leq x <   \frac {1}{2} \\ [ 0, 1 ], & x = 1 / 2 \\ \{1 \}, & \frac {1}{2} <   x \leq 1 \end{array} \right.
$$

is convex-valued and upper hemicontinuous on $[ 0 , 1 ]$ , while it is not lower hemicontinuous at $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } }$ . It is easily checked that, for small enough $\varepsilon > 0$ , no $f \in { \bf C } [ 0 , 1 ]$ satisfies $d _ { 2 } ( f ( x ) , \Psi ( { \bar { x } } ) ) < \varepsilon$ for all $x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ 

The Approximate Selection Lemma identifies certain conditions on a correspondence Ψ that allows us to find a continuous function, the graph of which lies arbitrarily near to that of the correspondence. Of course, one way of finding such a function is to look for a continuous f the graph of which lies entirely in that of Ψ, for then we would have $d _ { 2 } ( f ( x ) , \Psi ( x ) ) = 0$ for all x. Unfortunately, this is too much to ask from the postulates of the Approximate Selection Lemma. (Really?) As we show next, however, the situation is quite satisfactory for closed-valued correspondences. 

Michael’s Selection Theorem. For any given $n \in \mathbb { N } ,$ , let X be a nonempty, closed, bounded and convex subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , and $\Psi : X  \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ a convex- and closed-valued lower hemicontinuous correspondence. Then, there exists an $f \in \mathbf { C } ( X , \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ ) such that $f ( x ) \in \Psi ( x )$ for each $x \in X$ 

Proof. By the Approximate Selection Lemma, there exists an $f _ { 1 } \in \mathbf { C } ( X , \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ with $d _ { 2 } ( f _ { 1 } ( x ) , \Psi ( x ) ) < \frac { 1 } { 2 }$ for each $x \in X$ . Define $\Psi _ { 2 } : X  \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ by 

$$
\Psi_ {2} (x) := \Psi (x) \cap \left\{y: d _ {2} (y, f _ {1} (x)) <   \frac {1}{2} \right\}.
$$

(Why is $\Psi _ { 2 }$ well-defined?) $\Psi _ { 2 }$ is easily checked to be convex-valued and lower hemicontinuous. (Verify!) Apply the Approximate Selection Lemma again to get an $f _ { 2 } \in \mathbf { C } ( X , \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ with $\begin{array} { r } { d _ { 2 } ( f _ { 2 } ( x ) , \Psi _ { 2 } ( x ) ) < \frac { 1 } { 4 } } \end{array}$ for each $x \in X$ , and define 

$$
\Psi_ {3} (x) := \Psi (x) \cap \left\{y \in \mathbb {R} ^ {n}: d _ {2} (y, f _ {2} (x)) <   \frac {1}{4} \right\}, \quad x \in X.
$$

Proceeding by induction, we find a sequence $\left( f _ { m } \right)$ in $\mathbf { C } ( X , \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ such that, for each $m = 2 , 3 , . . . ,$ 

$$
d _ {2} (f _ {m} (x), \Psi_ {m} (x)) <   \frac {1}{2 ^ {m}} \quad \text { for   all } x \in X\tag{21}
$$

where 

$$
\Psi_ {m} (x) := \Psi (x) \cap \left\{y \in \mathbb {R} ^ {n}: d _ {2} (y, f _ {m - 1} (x)) <   \frac {1}{2 ^ {m - 1}} \right\}, \quad x \in X.
$$

We claim that $\left( f _ { m } \right)$ is Cauchy in $\mathbf { C } ( X , \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ . Indeed, by construction, for each $x \in X$ and $m \geq 2$ , there exists a $y ^ { m } \in \Psi _ { m } ( x )$ such that 

$$
d _ {2} (f _ {m} (x), f _ {m - 1} (x)) \leq d _ {2} (f _ {m} (x), y ^ {m}) + d _ {2} (y ^ {m}, f _ {m - 1} (x)) <   \frac {1}{2 ^ {m}} + \frac {1}{2 ^ {m - 1}} = \frac {3}{2 ^ {m}}.
$$

Therefore, for any $k > l$ and any $x \in X$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} d _ {2} (f _ {k} (x), f _ {l} (x)) & \leq & d _ {2} (f _ {k} (x), f _ {k - 1} (x)) + \dots + d _ {2} (f _ {l + 1} (x), f _ {l} (x)) \\ & <   & \frac {3}{2 ^ {k}} + \dots + \frac {3}{2 ^ {l + 1}} \\ & <   & 3 \sum_ {i = l + 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {i}}, \end{array}
$$

so we have $\operatorname* { s u p } \{ d _ { 2 } ( f _ { k } ( x ) , f _ { l } ( x ) ) : x \in X \} \to 0$ as $l  \infty$ . Hence, since $\mathbf { C } ( X , \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ is complete (Exercise D.45), there exists an $f \in \mathbf { C } ( X , \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ such that $f _ { m } \to f .$ . Now fix an arbitrary $x \in X$ , and note that, thanks to (21), for each m N there is a $y ^ { m } \in \Psi _ { m } ( x ) \subseteq \Psi ( x )$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { d _ { 2 } ( f _ { m } ( x ) , y ^ { m } ) < \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { m } } } \end{array}$ . Since $f _ { m } ( x )  f ( x )$ , therefore, we must have $y ^ { m } \to f ( x )$ . (Why?) Since $\Psi ( x )$ is a closed set, then, we conclude: $f ( x ) \in \Psi ( x )$ 

When combined with the Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem, Michael’s Selection Theorem yields the following result that shows that in Kakutani’s Fixed Point Theorem the closed graph property can be replaced with closed-valuedness and lower hemicontinuity. 

Corollary 1. (Michael) For any given $n \in \mathbb { N } ,$ , let X be a nonempty, closed, bounded and convex subset of R<sup>n</sup>. If Ψ is a convex- and closed-valued lower hemicontinuous self-correspondence on $X$ , then it has a fixed point. 

This does cover ground that is missed by Kakutani’s Fixed Point Theorem. For instance, the convex- and closed-valued lower hemicontinuous self-correspondence Γ defined on $[ 0 , 1 ]$ by $\Gamma ( 0 ) : = \{ 0 \}$ and $\Gamma ( x ) : = [ 0 , 1 ]$ for all $x \in ( 0 , 1 ]$ , is not upper hemicontinuous. 

Warning. Convex-valuedness is essential for Michael’s Selection Theorem and Corollary 1. The self-correspondence Γ defined on [0, 1] as $\Gamma ( 0 ) : = \{ 1 \} , \Gamma ( 1 ) : = \{ 0 \}$ and $\Gamma ( x ) : = \{ 0 , 1 \}$ for all $0 < x < 1$ , is closed-valued and lower hemicontinuous, but it does not admit a continuous selection. 

Exercise 61. Define $g : [ - 1 , 1 ] \to [ 0 , 1 ]$ and $\Psi : [ - 1 , 1 ]  [ 0 , 1 ]$ by

$$

Show that there exists an $\mathcal { F } \subseteq \mathbf { C } ( X , \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ such that $\Psi ( x ) = \{ F ( x ) : F \in { \mathcal { F } } \}$ for all $x \in X$
